quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The bakery ___ fresh croissants at dawn.
quests.completedSentence: The bakery bakes fresh croissants at dawn.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The bakery' names one single business, so it counts as a third-person singular subject. In the simple present, singular subjects take a verb ending in -s or -es, which is why 'bakes' is correct here.
quests.nativeTip: Find the one thing performing the action here, then decide if it needs the -s ending.
quests.example: The bakery bakes fresh croissants at dawn.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: My neighbor ___ his lawn every Saturday.
quests.completedSentence: My neighbor mows his lawn every Saturday.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My neighbor' refers to one person, so the sentence needs the singular verb form. 'Mows' carries the -s ending that marks agreement with a singular, third-person subject.
quests.nativeTip: Ask yourself how many neighbors are doing the action before choosing the verb form.
quests.example: My neighbor mows his lawn every Saturday.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The printer ___ documents for the whole office.
quests.completedSentence: The printer prints documents for the whole office.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The printer' is a single machine, which makes it a singular subject. Singular subjects in the simple present need the -s form of the verb, so 'prints' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Decide whether 'the printer' is one machine or several before picking the verb.
quests.example: The printer prints documents for the whole office.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The interns ___ coffee for the team every afternoon.
quests.completedSentence: The interns make coffee for the team every afternoon.
quests.grammarRule: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The interns' is a plural subject, since more than one intern is involved. Plural subjects in the simple present use the base form of the verb, so 'make' is correct, not 'makes'.
quests.nativeTip: Notice that 'interns' already ends in -s as a noun - that's a clue about how many people we're talking about.
quests.example: The interns make coffee for the team every afternoon.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Local farmers ___ their vegetables at the weekend market.
quests.completedSentence: Local farmers sell their vegetables at the weekend market.
quests.grammarRule: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Local farmers' describes more than one person, so it's a plural subject. Plural subjects take the base verb form in the simple present, which makes 'sell' the right choice.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether the subject names one farmer or a group of them.
quests.example: Local farmers sell their vegetables at the weekend market.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The passengers ___ their tickets before boarding.
quests.completedSentence: The passengers show their tickets before boarding.
quests.grammarRule: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The passengers' is plural, referring to multiple travelers. Because the subject is plural, the verb keeps its base form: 'show', without an -s ending.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the noun right before the blank and decide if it's one person or many.
quests.example: The passengers show their tickets before boarding.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: She ___ the accounts for a small business.
quests.completedSentence: She manages the accounts for a small business.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'She' is a third-person singular pronoun, so the verb must take the -s ending in the simple present. 'Manages' is correct; 'manage' would only work with a plural subject.
quests.nativeTip: 'She' always refers to one person - think about what that means for the verb ending.
quests.example: She manages the accounts for a small business.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: He ___ his bike to campus most days.
quests.completedSentence: He rides his bike to campus most days.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'He' is singular and third-person, so the verb needs the -s form: 'rides'. Without the -s, the sentence would no longer agree with the subject.
quests.nativeTip: Remember that 'he' behaves the same way as 'she' for verb endings.
quests.example: He rides his bike to campus most days.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: After the meeting, she ___ a short summary to the team.
quests.completedSentence: After the meeting, she sends a short summary to the team.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: The opening phrase 'after the meeting' doesn't affect agreement; the subject is still 'she', which is singular. That means the verb needs -s: 'sends'.
quests.nativeTip: Don't let the introductory phrase distract you - focus on who 'she' is.
quests.example: After the meeting, she sends a short summary to the team.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: This clinic sees many patients. It ___ appointments online too.
quests.completedSentence: This clinic sees many patients. It accepts appointments online too.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'It' refers back to 'this clinic', a singular subject, so the verb takes the -s ending: 'accepts'. Pronouns like 'it' follow the same singular agreement pattern as 'he' and 'she'.
quests.nativeTip: 'It' stands in for a single place or thing already mentioned - treat it like 'he' or 'she'.
quests.example: This clinic sees many patients. It accepts appointments online too.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The washing machine broke last week. It ___ strange noises now.
quests.completedSentence: The washing machine broke last week. It makes strange noises now.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'It' refers to 'the washing machine', a single object, so the subject is singular. Singular subjects require the -s ending, which is why 'makes' is correct here.
quests.nativeTip: Identify what 'it' is replacing before deciding on the verb form.
quests.example: The washing machine broke last week. It makes strange noises now.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: It ___ heavily during the monsoon season here.
quests.completedSentence: It rains heavily during the monsoon season here.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun 'it' in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: In weather expressions, 'it' is a fixed singular subject with no real-world referent. It still follows the singular agreement rule, so the verb takes -s: 'rains'.
quests.nativeTip: This 'it' doesn't replace a noun at all - it's the weather subject, and it still counts as singular.
quests.example: It rains heavily during the monsoon season here.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: We ___ groceries online to save time.
quests.completedSentence: We order groceries online to save time.
quests.grammarRule: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' is a plural pronoun, so the verb stays in its base form: 'order'. Adding -s would incorrectly treat the subject as singular.
quests.nativeTip: 'We' always includes more than one person, no matter the context.
quests.example: We order groceries online to save time.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: They ___ the museum every year during the school trip.
quests.completedSentence: They visit the museum every year during the school trip.
quests.grammarRule: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'They' is a plural pronoun, so it pairs with the base verb form: 'visit'. 'Visits' would only be correct with a singular subject like 'he' or 'she'.
quests.nativeTip: 'They' is never singular, so check which verb form matches a plural subject.
quests.example: They visit the museum every year during the school trip.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: After work, we ___ a short walk around the block.
quests.completedSentence: After work, we take a short walk around the block.
quests.grammarRule: Plural pronoun (we/they) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject here is still 'we', a plural pronoun, regardless of the introductory phrase. Plural subjects use the base verb form, so 'take' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase at the start doesn't change who the subject is - look at the pronoun.
quests.example: After work, we take a short walk around the block.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The security guard ___ the entrance at night.
quests.completedSentence: The security guard watches the entrance at night.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The security guard' is singular, and the verb 'watch' ends in -ch, so it takes -es instead of just -s: 'watches'. This spelling rule applies to verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, -s, or -o.
quests.nativeTip: This verb ends in a sound that needs an extra syllable before adding -s - think -es, not just -s.
quests.example: The security guard watches the entrance at night.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The chef ___ the vegetables before every dinner service.
quests.completedSentence: The chef washes the vegetables before every dinner service.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The chef' is a singular subject, and since 'wash' ends in -sh, it needs the -es ending rather than a simple -s: 'washes'.
quests.nativeTip: Look at how the verb ends, then decide whether -s alone is enough.
quests.example: The chef washes the vegetables before every dinner service.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The mechanic ___ engine problems quickly.
quests.completedSentence: The mechanic fixes engine problems quickly.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -x, or -s add -es for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The mechanic' is singular, and 'fix' ends in -x, so the singular form adds -es: 'fixes'. Just adding -s would be spelled incorrectly for this verb.
quests.nativeTip: Check the last letter of the verb before choosing between -s and -es.
quests.example: The mechanic fixes engine problems quickly.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The children ___ board games after school.
quests.completedSentence: The children play board games after school.
quests.grammarRule: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Children' is the irregular plural form of 'child'. Even though it doesn't end in -s, it's still a plural subject, so the verb stays in its base form: 'play'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Children' looks nothing like a regular plural noun, but it still behaves like one for the verb.
quests.example: The children play board games after school.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Many people ___ this park for morning runs.
quests.completedSentence: Many people use this park for morning runs.
quests.grammarRule: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.ruleExplanation: 'People' is the irregular plural of 'person' and always takes a plural verb form. That's why 'use' is correct instead of 'uses'.
quests.nativeTip: 'People' is already plural in meaning, even without an -s ending.
quests.example: Many people use this park for morning runs.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The women in this club ___ marathons together every spring.
quests.completedSentence: The women in this club run marathons together every spring.
quests.grammarRule: Irregular plural nouns take the plural (base) verb form
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Women' is the irregular plural of 'woman', so it's a plural subject and needs the base verb form: 'run', not 'runs'.
quests.nativeTip: Think about what 'women' is the plural of, and match the verb accordingly.
quests.example: The women in this club run marathons together every spring.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The delivery driver ___ packages across the city.
quests.completedSentence: The delivery driver carries packages across the city.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The delivery driver' is singular, and 'carry' ends in a consonant + y, so the singular form changes the y to i and adds -es: 'carries'.
quests.nativeTip: This verb ends in a consonant plus -y - that spelling changes in the singular form.
quests.example: The delivery driver carries packages across the city.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: My cousin ___ for a scholarship every year.
quests.completedSentence: My cousin applies for a scholarship every year.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My cousin' is a singular subject, and since 'apply' ends in consonant + y, the singular form is 'applies', with the y changed to i before -es.
quests.nativeTip: Check the ending of 'apply' before deciding how the singular form is spelled.
quests.example: My cousin applies for a scholarship every year.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.sentenceWithBlank: This bakery chain ___ new recipes every season.
quests.completedSentence: This bakery chain tries new recipes every season.
quests.grammarRule: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies for singular subjects
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This bakery chain' functions as one singular entity, and 'try' ends in consonant + y, so the singular form is 'tries', not 'try'.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the -y ending on the verb, and remember how that changes for singular subjects.
quests.example: This bakery chain tries new recipes every season.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The volunteers at the shelter ___ the animals twice a day.
quests.completedSentence: The volunteers at the shelter feed the animals twice a day.
quests.grammarRule: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject is 'the volunteers', a plural noun, even though 'the shelter' appears nearby. Plural subjects take the base verb form, so 'feed' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Don't stop at the first noun - find the word that's actually doing the action.
quests.example: The volunteers at the shelter feed the animals twice a day.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The volunteer at the front desk ___ visitors with a smile.
quests.completedSentence: The volunteer at the front desk greets visitors with a smile.
quests.grammarRule: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.ruleExplanation: Here 'the volunteer' is singular, unlike the plural 'volunteers' in a similar sentence. A singular subject needs the -s ending, so 'greets' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Compare this subject carefully with a similar-looking plural one - singular or plural this time?
quests.example: The volunteer at the front desk greets visitors with a smile.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Local museums ___ free admission on the first Sunday of the month.
quests.completedSentence: Local museums offer free admission on the first Sunday of the month.
quests.grammarRule: Subject-verb agreement based on singular vs. plural noun form
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Local museums' is plural, so the verb takes the base form: 'offer'. The -s ending would incorrectly suggest a singular subject.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the plural ending on the subject noun before choosing the verb.
quests.example: Local museums offer free admission on the first Sunday of the month.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The tourists ___ photos of the old lighthouse every summer.
quests.completedSentence: The tourists take photos of the old lighthouse every summer.
quests.grammarRule: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The tourists' is a plural subject, so it takes the base verb form: 'take'. This combines the noun-recognition and plural-verb rules covered throughout this stage.
quests.nativeTip: Review what you've learned so far: is this subject one person or several?
quests.example: The tourists take photos of the old lighthouse every summer.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: She ___ the lighthouse tours on weekends.
quests.completedSentence: She leads the lighthouse tours on weekends.
quests.grammarRule: Third-person singular pronoun (he/she) in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'She' is singular and third-person, so the verb needs the -s ending: 'leads'. This is the same rule you practiced with 'he' and 'she' earlier.
quests.nativeTip: Bring back what you know about singular pronouns to choose the verb here.
quests.example: She leads the lighthouse tours on weekends.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.sentenceWithBlank: Local guides ___ visitors about the lighthouse's history.
quests.completedSentence: Local guides teach visitors about the lighthouse's history.
quests.grammarRule: Plural subject in the simple present
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Local guides' is a plural subject, so the verb stays in its base form: 'teach'. Recognizing plural nouns like this is the foundation for every stage ahead.
quests.nativeTip: As a final check, decide if 'guides' here is doing the action as one person or many.
quests.example: Local guides teach visitors about the lighthouse's history.
